claim: A whole-genome CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen was performed in H4 human neuroglioma cells expressing endogenous LC3B tagged with tandem GFP and mCherry.
source: To identify novel autophagy regulators, we performed a whole-genome CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen in H4 human neuroglioma cells expressing endogenous LC3B tagged with a tandem of GFP and mCherry.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methodology used in the study, including the cell line and screening approach.

claim: UBA6 and BIRC6 were identified as autophagy regulators in the CRISPR/Cas9 screen.
source: Using this methodology, we identified the ubiquitin-activating enzyme UBA6 and the hybrid ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme/ubiquitin ligase BIRC6 as autophagy regulators.
evidence: The screen results identified these specific proteins as regulators.

claim: UBA6 and BIRC6 cooperate to monoubiquitinate LC3B.
source: We found that these enzymes cooperate to monoubiquitinate LC3B, targeting it for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing the enzymatic cooperation and monoubiquitination.

claim: Monoubiquitinated LC3B is targeted for proteasomal degradation.
source: We found that these enzymes cooperate to monoubiquitinate LC3B, targeting it for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: The manuscript shows that monoubiquitination leads to proteasomal degradation through experimental data.

claim: Knockout of UBA6 or BIRC6 increased autophagic flux under conditions of nutrient deprivation.
source: Knockout of UBA6 or BIRC6 increased autophagic flux under conditions of nutrient deprivation or protein synthesis inhibition.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing increased autophagic flux in knockout cells under starvation conditions.

claim: Knockout of UBA6 or BIRC6 increased autophagic flux under conditions of protein synthesis inhibition.
source: Knockout of UBA6 or BIRC6 increased autophagic flux under conditions of nutrient deprivation or protein synthesis inhibition.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing increased autophagic flux in knockout cells under protein synthesis inhibition.

claim: UBA6 or BIRC6 depletion decreased the formation of aggresome-like induced structures in H4 cells.
source: Moreover, UBA6 or BIRC6 depletion decreased the formation of aggresome-like induced structures in H4 cells, and α-synuclein aggregates in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing decreased ALIS formation in knockout cells.

claim: UBA6 or BIRC6 depletion decreased α-synuclein aggregates in rat hippocampal neurons.
source: Moreover, UBA6 or BIRC6 depletion decreased the formation of aggresome-like induced structures in H4 cells, and α-synuclein aggregates in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing decreased α-synuclein aggregates in neurons with depleted UBA6 or BIRC6.

claim: UBA6 and BIRC6 negatively regulate autophagy by limiting the availability of LC3B.
source: These findings demonstrate that UBA6 and BIRC6 negatively regulate autophagy by limiting the availability of LC3B.
evidence: The manuscript presents multiple lines of experimental evidence supporting this regulatory mechanism.

claim: Inhibition of UBA6/BIRC6 could be used to enhance autophagic clearance of protein aggregates in neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Inhibition of UBA6/BIRC6 could be used to enhance autophagic clearance of protein aggregates in neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic application based on the experimental findings.

claim: Autophagy is a catabolic process involving the engulfment of cytoplasmic materials into double-membraned autophagosomes that subsequently fuse with lysosomes.
source: Macroautophagy (herein referred to as autophagy) is a catabolic process involving the engulfment of cytoplasmic materials into double-membraned autophagosomes that subsequently fuse with lysosomes to form autolysosomes, where the materials are degraded by acid hydrolases (Bento et al., 2016; Dikic and Elazar, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Autophagy substrates include protein aggregates, damaged organelles and intracellular pathogens.
source: Autophagy substrates include abnormal particles such as protein aggregates, damaged organelles and intracellular pathogens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about autophagy substrates.

claim: Autophagy is involved in the degradation of normal cellular constituents for survival under conditions of nutrient restriction or other stresses.
source: Autophagy is also involved in the degradation of normal cellular constituents for survival under conditions of nutrient restriction or other stresses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about autophagy function.

claim: Defective autophagy contributes to the pathogenesis of neurodegeneration, cancer, cardiomyopathies and infectious diseases.
source: Defective autophagy contributes to the pathogenesis of various disorders, including neurodegeneration, cancer, cardiomyopathies and infectious diseases (Dikic and Elazar, 2018; Levine and Kroemer, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LC3B is the best studied member of the Atg8 family.
source: The best studied member of this family is LC3B (product of the MAP1LC3B gene), which undergoes conversion from a soluble, cytosolic form (LC3B-I) to a phosphatidylethanolamine (PE)-conjugated, membrane-bound form (LC3B-II) (Kabeya et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LC3B undergoes conversion from a soluble, cytosolic form (LC3B-I) to a phosphatidylethanolamine (PE)-conjugated, membrane-bound form (LC3B-II).
source: The best studied member of this family is LC3B (product of the MAP1LC3B gene), which undergoes conversion from a soluble, cytosolic form (LC3B-I) to a phosphatidylethanolamine (PE)-conjugated, membrane-bound form (LC3B-II) (Kabeya et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LC3B-II interacts with LC3-interacting region (LIR) motifs of various cargo receptors to capture autophagic cargos into forming autophagosomes.
source: LC3B-II subsequently interacts with LC3-interacting region (LIR) motifs of various cargo receptors to capture autophagic cargos into forming autophagosomes (Birgisdottir et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SQSTM1 (p62), NBR1, NDP52, OPTN and TAX1BP1 are cytosolic cargo receptors that bind polyubiquitinated cargos via their Ub-binding domains.
source: Among these receptors are cytosolic proteins such as SQSTM1 (p62), NBR1, NDP52, OPTN and TAX1BP1, which bind polyubiquitinated cargos via their Ub-binding domains (Birgisdottir et al., 2013; Wild et al., 2014; Johansen and Lamark, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: BNIP3, NIX and FUNDC1 are cargo receptors anchored to mitochondria via their transmembrane domains in mitophagy.
source: Other cargo receptors are anchored to the autophagic cargos via their transmembrane domains, as is the case for BNIP3, NIX and FUNDC1 in mitochondrial autophagy (mitophagy) (Birgisdottir et al., 2013; Wild et al., 2014; Johansen and Lamark, 2019)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RTN3, SEC62, CCPG1, FAM134B and TEX264 are cargo receptors in ER-phagy.
source: and RTN3, SEC62, CCPG1, FAM134B and TEX264 in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) autophagy (ER-phagy) (Khaminets et al., 2015; Fumagalli et al., 2016; Grumati et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2018; Chino et al., 2019; Johansen and Lamark, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: After fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes, the autophagy cargos, together with the Atg8-family proteins and cargo receptors, are degraded in lysosomes.
source: After fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes, the autophagy cargos, together with the Atg8-family proteins and cargo receptors, are degraded in lysosomes (Tanida et al., 2005; Bjørkøy et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LC3B interacts with the LIR motif of FYCO1, which serves as an adaptor to the kinesin-1 motor, enabling anterograde transport of autophagosomes along microtubule tracks.
source: In addition to participating in cargo recruitment to the forming autophagosome, LC3B interacts with the LIR motif of FYCO1 (FYVE and coiled-coil domain containing protein 1), which serves as an adaptor to the kinesin-1 motor, enabling anterograde transport of autophagosomes along microtubule tracks (Pankiv et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LC3B interacts with the LIR motif of PLEKHM1, which functions as a tether in autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: Furthermore, LC3B interacts with the LIR motif of another adaptor protein, PLEKHM1 (pleckstrin homology domain containing protein family member 1), which functions as a tether in autophagosome-lysosome fusion (McEwan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ULK1 phosphorylates VPS34, BECN1 and ATG14L1 components of the class III PI3K complex.
source: As an example of positive regulation, the unc-51-like autophagy-activating kinase 1 (ULK1) phosphorylates the VPS34 (Egan et al., 2015; Russell et al., 2013), BECN1 (Russell et al., 2013) and ATG14L1 (Park et al., 2016) components of the class III PI3K complex
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The class III PI3K complex catalyzes the conversion of phosphatidylinositol (PI) to phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate [PI(3)P], triggering phagophore formation.
source: which subsequently catalyzes the conversion of phosphatidylinositol (PI) to phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate [PI(3)P], thus triggering phagophore formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PI3K complex function.

claim: ULK1 is activated by phosphorylation on Ser-317, Ser-555 and Ser-777 by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
source: ULK1 itself is activated by phosphorylation on Ser-317, Ser-555 and Ser-777 by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Egan et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mTORC1 kinase negatively regulates autophagy by phosphorylating ULK1 on Ser-757, preventing the interaction of ULK1 with AMPK.
source: On the other hand, the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex-1 (mTORC1) kinase negatively regulates autophagy by phosphorylating ULK1 on Ser-757, and thus preventing the interaction of ULK1 with AMPK (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: mTORC1 kinase exerts an additional inhibitory effect on autophagy by phosphorylating UVRAG, decreasing autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: The mTORC1 kinase exerts an additional inhibitory effect on autophagy by phosphorylating the autophagy protein UVRAG, a modification that decreases autophagosome maturation and autophagosome-lysosome fusion (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ULK1 and BECN1 are positively regulated by polyubiquitination mediated by the Ub-ligase TRAF6.
source: For instance, ULK1 and BECN1 are positively regulated by polyubiquitination mediated by the Ub-ligase (E3) TRAF6 (Shi and Kehrl, 2010; Nazio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Polyubiquitination of OPTN by the E3 HACE1 promotes assembly of OPTN with SQSTM1 and results in enhanced autophagic degradation.
source: Non-enzymatic components of the autophagy machinery can also be positively regulated by ubiquitination, as is the case for the polyubiquitination of OPTN by the E3 HACE1, which promotes assembly of OPTN with SQSTM1 and thus results in enhanced autophagic degradation (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TRAF6-mediated polyubiquitination of mTOR activates mTORC1, inhibiting autophagy.
source: An example of the negative effects of ubiquitination on autophagy is the activation of mTORC1 by TRAF6-mediated polyubiquitination of the catalytic mTOR subunit, with consequent inhibition of autophagy (Linares et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ULK1 and components of the class III PI3K complex are targeted for polyubiquitination and degradation by the E3 Cul3-KLHL20.
source: Furthermore, ULK1 and components of the class III PI3K complex are targeted for polyubiquitination and degradation by the E3 Cul3-KLHL20 (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: BECN1 is polyubiquitinated by the RNF216 and NEDD4 E3s, causing destabilization of the class III PI3K complex.
source: Finally, BECN1 is polyubiquitinated by the RNF216 and NEDD4 E3s, causing destabilization of the class III PI3K complex (Platta et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin or torin1 is widely used to stimulate autophagy.
source: For example, inhibition of mTORC1 by the drugs rapamycin or torin1 (Noda and Ohsumi, 1998; Thoreen et al., 2009), or activation of AMPK by metformin (Shi et al., 2012), are widely used to stimulate autophagy.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Activation of AMPK by metformin is widely used to stimulate autophagy.
source: For example, inhibition of mTORC1 by the drugs rapamycin or torin1 (Noda and Ohsumi, 1998; Thoreen et al., 2009), or activation of AMPK by metformin (Shi et al., 2012), are widely used to stimulate autophagy.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Inhibition of the class III PI3K complex by wortmannin, LY294002 or 3-methyladenine impairs autophagy.
source: In contrast, inhibition of the class III PI3K complex by wortmannin, LY294002 or 3-methyladenine impairs autophagy (Blommaart et al., 1997; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Inhibition of USP10/13-mediated deubiquitination of BECN1 by spautin-1 causes destabilization and degradation of the class III PI3K complex, decreasing autophagy.
source: Finally, inhibition of USP10/13-mediated deubiquitination of BECN1 by spautin-1 causes destabilization and degradation of the class III PI3K complex, decreasing autophagy (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Autophagy stimulation has been proposed as a possible therapy for neurodegenerative disorders caused by accumulation of intracellular protein aggregates.
source: Autophagy stimulation has been proposed as a possible therapy for neurodegenerative disorders caused by accumulation of intracellular protein aggregates (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed therapeutic application supported by citation.

claim: Autophagy inhibition could be used to treat hyperproliferative disorders fueled by increased autophagy, as is the case for some cancers.
source: Autophagy inhibition, on the other hand, could be used to treat hyperproliferative disorders fueled by increased autophagy, as is the case for some cancers (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposed therapeutic application supported by citation.

claim: The involvement of known regulators of autophagy in other cellular processes has hampered efforts to exploit their pharmacologic activation or inhibition for clinical uses.
source: However, the involvement of known regulators of autophagy in other cellular processes has hampered efforts to exploit their pharmacologic activation or inhibition for clinical uses.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in the field.

claim: The H4-tfLC3B cell line was made by gene-editing human neuroglioma H4 cells to express endogenous LC3B tagged at its N-terminus with tandem GFP and mCherry fluorescent proteins.
source: This cell line, named H4-tfLC3B (H4-tandem fluorescent LC3B), was made by gene-editing human neuroglioma H4 cells to express endogenous LC3B tagged at its N-terminus with tandem GFP and mCherry fluorescent proteins (designated GFP-mCherry-LC3B) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of the cell line and references a figure showing the methodology.

claim: The quenching of GFP, and not mCherry, in the acidic pH of autolysosomes allows the use of the GFP:mCherry ratio to monitor autophagy flux.
source: The quenching of GFP, and not mCherry, in the acidic pH of autolysosomes allows the use of the GFP:mCherry ratio to monitor the delivery of GFP-mCherry-LC3B from neutral autophagosomes to acidic autolysosomes (process referred to as 'autophagy flux') (Kimura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established methodology supported by citation.

claim: Endogenous tagging avoids the overexpression artifacts caused by transfection of cells with plasmids encoding fluorescently tagged LC3B.
source: Moreover, endogenous tagging avoids the overexpression artifacts caused by transfection of cells with plasmids encoding fluorescently tagged LC3B (Kimura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a methodological advantage supported by citation.

claim: Live-cell imaging of H4-tfLC3B cells revealed puncta displaying both GFP and mCherry fluorescence (autophagosomes), or only mCherry fluorescence (autolysosomes).
source: Live-cell imaging of H4-tfLC3B cells revealed puncta displaying both GFP and mCherry fluorescence (i.e., autophagosomes), or only mCherry fluorescence (i.e., autolysosomes) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing these puncta.

claim: Treatment of H4-tfLC3B cells with bafilomycin A1 increased the number of puncta containing GFP in addition to mCherry.
source: Treatment of these cells with the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) inhibitor bafilomycin A1 increased the number of puncta containing GFP in addition to mCherry (Figure 1A)
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing this effect.

claim: Treatment of H4-tfLC3B cells with bafilomycin A1 increased the GFP:mCherry ratio in FACS analyses.
source: Treatment of these cells with the vacuolar ATPase (v-ATPase) inhibitor bafilomycin A1 increased the number of puncta containing GFP in addition to mCherry (Figure 1A), as well as the GFP:mCherry ratio in FACS analyses (seen as a displacement to the right in Figure 1B)
evidence: The manuscript presents FACS data showing this effect.

claim: siRNA-mediated knock down of ATG7 increased the GFP:mCherry ratio in H4-tfLC3B cells.
source: Likewise, siRNA-mediated knock down (KD) of the autophagy protein ATG7 increased the GFP:mCherry ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing this effect.

claim: Depletion of serum and amino acids from the medium decreased the GFP:mCherry ratio detected by FACS.
source: In contrast, depletion of serum and amino acids from the medium (i.e., nutrient deprivation) decreased the GFP:mCherry ratio detected by FACS (seen as a shift to the left in Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: The manuscript presents FACS data showing this effect.

claim: Most of the top-ranked genes in the primary screen corresponded to known components of the core autophagy machinery.
source: Most of the top-ranked genes in this analysis corresponded to known components of the core autophagy machinery (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 2) (Bento et al., 2016), demonstrating the reliability of the screen.
evidence: The manuscript presents screen results and references a figure showing the top hits.

claim: Previously reported autophagy effectors and regulators identified in the screen included MEF2BNB and SNAPIN subunits of BORC.
source: A number of previously reported autophagy effectors and regulators were also identified with lower but still significant scores; these included the MEF2BNB and SNAPIN subunits of BORC (Pu et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2017)
evidence: The manuscript presents screen results identifying these proteins.

claim: Previously reported autophagy effectors and regulators identified in the screen included C18orf8, BECN1, RAB1A, EPG5 and CCZ1B.
source: these included the MEF2BNB and SNAPIN subunits of BORC (Pu et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2017), C18orf8 (Vaites et al., 2017), BECN1 (Liang et al., 1999), RAB1A (Webster et al., 2016), EPG5 (Wang et al., 2016) and CCZ1B (Vaites et al., 2017) (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents screen results identifying these proteins.

claim: UBA6 stood out as a gene with relatively high scores in both the primary and secondary screens that had not been previously implicated in autophagy.
source: UBA6, however, stood out as a gene with relatively high scores in both the primary (Figure 1F) and secondary screens (Figure 2B), and that had not been previously implicated in autophagy.
evidence: The manuscript presents screen results showing UBA6 scores.

claim: UBA6 KD caused 3–4–fold increases in the levels of LC3B-I without altering the levels of LC3B-II in H4 and HeLa cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed that UBA6 KD caused 3–4–fold increases in the levels of LC3B-I without altering the levels of LC3B-II in both cell lines (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing this effect.

claim: ATG7 KD increased the levels LC3B-I but decreased the levels of LC3B-II.
source: This was in contrast to ATG7 KD, which increased the levels LC3B-I but decreased the levels of LC3B-II (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing this effect.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 KO of UBA6 resulted in increased levels of LC3B-I and unchanged levels of LC3B-II.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 KO of UBA6 also resulted in increased levels of LC3B-I and unchanged levels of LC3B-II, a phenotype that was partially reversed by transfection with plasmids encoding UBA6 tagged at either the N- or C-terminus with the MYC epitope (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing this effect.

claim: Transfection of UBA6-KO cells with plasmids encoding MYC-UBA6 or UBA6-MYC partially reversed the increased LC3B-I phenotype.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 KO of UBA6 also resulted in increased levels of LC3B-I and unchanged levels of LC3B-II, a phenotype that was partially reversed by transfection with plasmids encoding UBA6 tagged at either the N- or C-terminus with the MYC epitope (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing this rescue effect.

claim: UBA6 KO caused a similar increase in the levels of LC3A-I but not of other Atg8-family members such as GABARAP and GABARAPL1.
source: UBA6 KO caused a similar increase in the levels of LC3A-I but not of other Atg8-family members such as GABARAP and GABARAPL1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing this specificity.

claim: UBA6 KO did not cause noticeable changes in the levels of other components of the autophagy machinery.
source: UBA6 KO did not cause noticeable changes in the levels of other components of the autophagy machinery, including components of the LC3-conjugation system (ATG3, ATG5, ATG7, ATG12, ATG16L1), WIPI2, the PI3K complex (BECN1, p-BECN1 and ATG14), the ULK1 complex (ATG13, p-ATG13, ULK1, p-ULK1), and the mTOR signaling pathway (S6K, p-S6K, 4EBP, p-4EBP, TSC2, p-TSC2, AKT, p-AKT) (Bento et al., 2016) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing no changes in these proteins.

claim: Fluorescent staining for SQSTM1, WIPI2 and ATG9A showed no differences in UBA6-KO cells relative to the parental H4 cells.
source: Likewise, fluorescent staining for the autophagy machinery components SQSTM1, WIPI2 and ATG9A (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C), and for markers of the ER (calnexin), Golgi complex (GM130), mitochondria (TOM20), early endosomes (RAB5, APPL1, EEA1), lysosomes (LAMP1, LAMTOR4) and the cytoskeleton (β-tubulin, F-actin) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–J), showed no differences in UBA6-KO cells relative to the parental H4 cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing no differences.

claim: UBA6-KO cells proliferated at the same rate as WT cells, with doubling times of ~27 hr.
source: In addition, we observed that UBA6-KO cells proliferated at the same rate as WT cells, with doubling times of ~27 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents cell proliferation data.

claim: Bafilomycin A1 treatment caused a similar accumulation of LC3B-II in WT, UBA6-KO cells and UBA6-KO cells rescued by transfection with a plasmid encoding UBA6-MYC.
source: Bafilomycin A1 treatment caused a similar accumulation of LC3B-II in WT, UBA6-KO cells and UBA6-KO cells rescued by transfection with a plasmid encoding UBA6-MYC (Figure 2G and H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C)
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing similar LC3B-II accumulation.

claim: WT and UBA6-KO cells expressing GFP-mCherry-LC3B and loaded with internalized Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated dextran exhibited similar ratios of autophagosomes to autolysosomes.
source: Finally, WT and UBA6-KO cells expressing GFP-mCherry-LC3B and loaded with internalized Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated dextran exhibited similar ratios of autophagosomes (i.e., puncta positive for GFP and mCherry, but negative for Alexa Fluor 647) to autolysosomes (i.e., puncta positive for mCherry and Alexa Fluor 647, but negative for GFP) (Figure 2I and J)
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing similar ratios.

claim: UBA6 KO had no effect on autophagosome-lysosome fusion and lysosome acidification.
source: indicating that UBA6 KO had no effect on autophagosome-lysosome fusion and lysosome acidification.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar ratios of autophagosomes to autolysosomes.

claim: KO of UBA6 did not change the levels of LC3B mRNA.
source: Real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) showed that KO of UBA6 did not change the levels of LC3B mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents RT-qPCR data showing no change in mRNA levels.

claim: Treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 resulted in a ~3 fold increase in the level of LC3B-I in WT H4 cells.
source: Indeed, treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 resulted in a ~3 fold increase in the level of LC3B-I in WT H4 cells, but did not change the already elevated level of LC3B-I in UBA6-KO cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing this increase.

claim: Treatment with MG132 did not change the already elevated level of LC3B-I in UBA6-KO cells.
source: Indeed, treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 resulted in a ~3 fold increase in the level of LC3B-I in WT H4 cells, but did not change the already elevated level of LC3B-I in UBA6-KO cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoblot data showing no change in UBA6-KO cells.

claim: Transgenic FLAG-tagged LC3B became conjugated with a single copy of HA-tagged Ub.
source: In addition, an in vivo ubiquitination assay showed that transgenic FLAG-tagged LC3B became conjugated with a single copy of HA-tagged Ub (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing monoubiquitination.

claim: The level of monoubiquitinated FLAG-LC3B was increased by treatment with MG132.
source: The level of monoubiquitinated FLAG-LC3B was increased by treatment with MG132 (Figure 3C)
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing increased monoubiquitination.

claim: The level of monoubiquitinated FLAG-LC3B was decreased by KO of UBA6.
source: and decreased by KO of UBA6 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing decreased monoubiquitination.

claim: Mutation of LC3B-I glycine-120 to alanine prevented the association of LC3B with autophagosomes.
source: Mutation of LC3B-I glycine-120 – the LC3B-I residue that is conjugated to phosphatidylethanolamine to produce LC3B-II (Kabeya et al., 2004) – to alanine prevented the association of LC3B with autophagosomes (Figure 3E)
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing lack of autophagosome association.

claim: Mutation of LC3B-I glycine-120 to alanine did not inhibit ubiquitination.
source: without inhibiting ubiquitination (Figure 3F)
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing ubiquitination of the mutant.

claim: LC3B can be ubiquitinated in the cytosol.
source: indicating that LC3B can be ubiquitinated in the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the ubiquitination of the G120A mutant that cannot associate with autophagosomes.

claim: FLAG-tagged LC3A and LC3C were also monoubiquitinated.
source: The in vivo ubiquitination assay was additionally used to show that FLAG-tagged LC3A and LC3C were also monoubiquitinated, but GABARAP, GABARAPL1 and GABARAPL2 were not (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing monoubiquitination of LC3A and LC3C.

claim: GABARAP, GABARAPL1 and GABARAPL2 were not monoubiquitinated.
source: The in vivo ubiquitination assay was additionally used to show that FLAG-tagged LC3A and LC3C were also monoubiquitinated, but GABARAP, GABARAPL1 and GABARAPL2 were not (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing lack of monoubiquitination.

claim: Endogenous LC3B was modified with a single HA-Ub moiety.
source: Finally, we found that endogenous LC3B was also modified with a single HA-Ub moiety (Figure 3H).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing monoubiquitination of endogenous LC3B.

claim: UBA6 promotes monoubiquitination of cytosolic LC3B-I, targeting it for degradation by the proteasome.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicated that UBA6 promotes monoubiquitination of cytosolic LC3B-I, targeting it for degradation by the proteasome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: Double K49R-K51R and single K51R mutants of LC3B were not ubiquitinated.
source: We observed that double K49R-K51R and single K51R mutants were not ubiquitinated, indicating that lysine-51 was the main ubiquitination site on LC3B (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing lack of ubiquitination of these mutants.

claim: Lysine-51 is the main ubiquitination site on LC3B.
source: We observed that double K49R-K51R and single K51R mutants were not ubiquitinated, indicating that lysine-51 was the main ubiquitination site on LC3B (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ubiquitination of K51R mutants.

claim: Lysine-51 is part of a hydrophobic pocket involved in the recognition of a LIR motif from the autophagy receptor SQSTM1.
source: Inspection of the structure of LC3B showed that lysine-51 is part of a hydrophobic pocket involved in the recognition of a LIR motif from the autophagy receptor SQSTM1 (Figure 4D) (Ichimura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and citation.

claim: The K51R substitution abolished the interaction of FLAG-LC3B with endogenous forms of SQSTM1 and NBR1.
source: Indeed, co-immunoprecipitation analyses showed that the K51R substitution abolished the interaction of FLAG-LC3B with endogenous forms of SQSTM1 and another autophagy receptor, NBR1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data showing loss of interaction.

claim: An additional function of LC3B ubiquitination by UBA6 may be to inhibit the recognition of autophagy receptors.
source: These results thus confirmed the critical function of lysine-51 in the recognition of autophagy receptors, and suggested that an additional function of LC3B ubiquitination by UBA6 may be to inhibit this recognition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: BIRC6 KO reduced LC3B ubiquitination to an even greater extent than UBA6 KO.
source: We observed that BIRC6 KO reduced LC3B ubiquitination to an even greater extent than UBA6 KO (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunoprecipitation data comparing ubiquitination levels.
